phil:nozick: Robert Nozick was an American political philosopher whose 1974 work Anarchy, State, and Utopia offered the most influential libertarian reply to John Rawls's egalitarian liberalism. He argued that only a minimal "night-watchman" state, limited to protecting people against force, theft, and fraud and to enforcing contracts, can be justified without violating individual rights, and he defended an entitlement theory of justice in which holdings are just if acquired and transferred through legitimate steps. Ranging far beyond politics, his later books such as Philosophical Explanations and The Examined Life addressed knowledge, personal identity, and the meaning of life with unusual breadth and inventiveness.
phil:sandel: Michael Sandel is an American political philosopher known for his communitarian critique of liberalism and for his enormously popular Harvard course on justice. In Liberalism and the Limits of Justice he challenged the Rawlsian idea of a self that exists prior to its ends, arguing instead that our identities are partly constituted by community attachments and shared conceptions of the good. Much of his later work, including What Money Can't Buy and The Tyranny of Merit, examines the moral limits of markets and the corrosive effects of a purely meritocratic society on solidarity and the common good.
phil:walzer: Michael Walzer is an American political theorist associated with communitarian and pluralist approaches to justice. In Spheres of Justice he argued for "complex equality," the view that different social goods—money, office, health care, political power—should be distributed according to their own distinct meanings and criteria, so that dominance in one sphere does not translate into dominance in others. He is also a leading figure in just war theory, whose Just and Unjust Wars revived a rights-based moral analysis of when and how wars may legitimately be fought.
phil:arendt: Hannah Arendt was a German-born political theorist who fled Nazism and became one of the twentieth century's most probing analysts of power, freedom, and evil. In The Origins of Totalitarianism she traced how movements like Nazism and Stalinism destroyed the space for common political life, while The Human Condition distinguished labor, work, and action and celebrated action and speech as the core of a genuinely public realm. Her report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann introduced the controversial phrase "the banality of evil," arguing that monstrous deeds can arise from thoughtless conformity rather than demonic intent.
phil:foucault: Michel Foucault was a French philosopher and historian whose work reshaped how power, knowledge, and the human subject are understood. Through studies of madness, medicine, prisons, and sexuality, he argued that what a society counts as truth is bound up with historically specific systems of power, and he introduced influential ideas such as disciplinary power, the panopticon, and biopolitics to describe how modern institutions shape and normalize individuals. Rather than treating human nature as fixed, he examined how categories like the criminal, the patient, and the sexual subject were produced by shifting discourses and practices.
phil:derrida: Jacques Derrida was a French philosopher and the founder of deconstruction, a mode of reading that exposes the unstable oppositions—speech and writing, presence and absence, nature and culture—on which Western thought rests. Beginning with works like Of Grammatology and Writing and Difference, he argued that meaning is never fully present but endlessly deferred through networks of difference, a movement he named with the coined term différance. His approach reshaped literary theory and philosophy alike, challenging the assumption that texts possess a single, stable, authorially guaranteed meaning.
phil:deleuze: Gilles Deleuze was a French philosopher who developed a wide-ranging metaphysics of difference, becoming, and multiplicity in opposition to philosophies grounded in fixed identity. In works such as Difference and Repetition he argued that difference is prior to identity, and in his celebrated collaborations with the psychoanalyst Félix Guattari, Anti-Oedipus and A Thousand Plateaus, he introduced concepts like the rhizome, assemblages, and desiring-production to describe reality as an open field of flows and connections. His readings of figures such as Spinoza, Nietzsche, and Bergson helped forge a creative, affirmative style of thought influential across philosophy and the arts.
phil:baudrillard: Jean Baudrillard was a French sociologist and theorist best known for his analyses of consumer society, media, and the collapse of reality into signs. He argued that late-capitalist culture is dominated by simulacra—copies without originals—so that images and models increasingly precede and replace the reality they once represented, a condition he called hyperreality. In works like Simulacra and Simulation he contended that the constant circulation of media images and codes has eroded any stable distinction between the real and its representation.
phil:lyotard: Jean-François Lyotard was a French philosopher most closely associated with the analysis of the postmodern condition. In his 1979 report The Postmodern Condition he defined the postmodern as "incredulity toward metanarratives," the loss of faith in the grand legitimating stories—progress, emancipation, the unity of knowledge—that had underwritten modern science and politics. Elsewhere, notably in The Differend, he explored conflicts between incommensurable discourses in which no shared rule of judgment can do justice to both parties, making the problem of injustice in language central to his thought.
phil:gramsci: Antonio Gramsci was an Italian Marxist theorist and political activist who reshaped Marxist thinking about culture and power while imprisoned under Mussolini's Fascist regime. In his Prison Notebooks he developed the concept of hegemony to explain how a ruling class maintains dominance not merely through force but by winning consent through cultural, moral, and intellectual leadership. He emphasized the role of civil society, ideology, and "organic intellectuals" in both sustaining and contesting the existing order, giving lasting impetus to cultural and political analysis on the left.
phil:marcuse: Herbert Marcuse was a German-American philosopher and a leading figure of the Frankfurt School of critical theory. Blending Marx and Freud, he argued that advanced industrial society pacifies dissent by manufacturing false needs and absorbing opposition, a condition he anatomized in One-Dimensional Man. In Eros and Civilization he imagined a non-repressive civilization in which technological abundance could liberate rather than dominate human desire, and his critiques of consumerism and conformity made him an intellectual touchstone for the New Left of the 1960s.
phil:adorno: Theodor Adorno was a German philosopher, sociologist, and musicologist central to the Frankfurt School's program of critical theory. With Max Horkheimer he wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment, which argued that the rationality meant to free humanity had turned into new forms of domination, and he coined the influential critique of the "culture industry" for reducing art to standardized, commodified entertainment. In Negative Dialectics and his aesthetic writings he defended non-identity thinking and difficult, uncompromising art as forms of resistance to a totally administered society.
phil:benjamin: Walter Benjamin was a German literary critic and philosopher whose eclectic work fused Marxism, Jewish mysticism, and a keen attention to modern culture. His essay "The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction" argued that technologies like photography and film strip artworks of their unique "aura" while opening new political possibilities for perception. In the unfinished Arcades Project and his theses "On the Concept of History" he read the debris of nineteenth-century commodity culture and reimagined history as a field of ruins and redemptive possibility rather than smooth progress.
phil:habermas: Jürgen Habermas is a German philosopher and social theorist, the most prominent second-generation member of the Frankfurt School. He is best known for his theory of communicative action, which locates the potential for reason and social coordination in everyday dialogue oriented toward mutual understanding, and for his historical account of the emergence and decline of the bourgeois public sphere. Through discourse ethics and his defense of deliberative democracy, he argues that legitimate norms are those that could win the rational agreement of all affected under conditions of free and open discussion.
phil:peirce: Charles Sanders Peirce was an American philosopher, logician, and scientist widely regarded as the founder of pragmatism. He proposed the "pragmatic maxim," according to which the meaning of a concept lies in the practical, experimental consequences we would expect it to have, and he made lasting contributions to logic, the theory of signs, and scientific method. Peirce also developed a broad system encompassing semiotics—his tripartite theory of signs—and a fallibilist view of inquiry as a self-correcting communal pursuit of truth over the long run.
